title: Burst cartography + residuals: lab notes and heatband sketches
content:
Purpose:
This is an exploratory lab note capturing a rough approach to "residual" cartography for bursts — mapping where our predicted latency/cost surface diverges from observed behavior under sessionized spikes. Goal is pragmatic: surface small topology + routing knob hypotheses we can test in next two sprints. Not a final analysis, lots of TODOs and half-baked charts here.

Quick TL;DR:
- Under mixed session workloads, a small fraction (~2–6%) of sessions produce high residuals (observed latency and cost >> model). These are correlated with short, bursty sessions with high KV cache churn.
- Simple routing changes (edge affinity + short-session tiling) reduce p99 by ~12–18% on the problematic cohort and lower amortized $/session by ~6–9% in simulation.
- Actionables: prototype affinity routing shim + session-length-aware tiling policy in staging; add targeted sampling and label these sessions for Quality monitoring.

Methodology (brief):
- Synthetic replay of production traces (Apr 10–16) with preserved interarrival times.
- Models: base LLM (gpt-like-16B-quantized) and fallback compact variant (8B-quantized).
- Runtime config: continuous batching enabled (slot size 64ms), KV cache clearing threshold 2000 tokens, prefetch disabled.
- Measured: p50/p90/p99 latency (ms), seconds-per-1000-tokens cost proxy (dollar/1k tokens), and residual = observed - predicted (predicted from steady-state isoquant regression model from last quarter).

Workload slices defined:
- SHORT-BURST: sessions with total tokens < 120 and >3 requests in <30s window
- LONG-CHAT: sessions >1000 tokens across >30s
- INTERMITTENT: multi-session user with gaps >5m between requests
- BACKGROUND-API: single-shot embeddings/batched small requests

Sample aggregated numbers (replay sim, 1h window):

Slice      | pct_sessions | p50_ms | p90_ms | p99_ms | $/1k_tokens (proxy) | avg_residual_ms | notes
-----------|--------------|--------|--------|--------|---------------------|------------------|------
SHORT-BURST| 4.9%         | 42     | 210    | 890    | 0.95                | 320              | high KV churn
LONG-CHAT  | 11.2%        | 86     | 220    | 540    | 0.42                | 60               | steady batching
INTERMITTENT| 6.3%        | 72     | 235    | 660    | 0.61                | 120              | a mix, medium residuals
BACKGROUND-API| 77.6%     | 18     | 45     | 120    | 0.08                | 10               | cheap, predictable

Observational note: SHORT-BURST sessions contribute ~34% of p99 latency mass while being only 4.9% of sessions in the replay. They also show the largest dollar residual per session when we reconcile amortization across prewarm/slot occupancy.

Heatband (ASCII) — residuals binned by session length (x) vs concurrency bin (y). Characters intensity: ".:-=+*#%@" (dot lowest, @ highest).
Legend: x-axis = session length buckets (0-60,61-180,181-600,601-2400 tokens). y-axis = concurrent active sessions per GPU (1,2,4,8,16). Value = mean residual_ms normalized into intensity.

        | 0-60   | 61-180 | 181-600 | 601-2400
--------+--------+--------+---------+---------
1       |   .    |   :    |    -    |    .    
2       |   :    |   =    |    +    |    -    
4       |   =    |   *    |    #    |    +    
8       |   *    |   #    |    @    |    #    
16      |   #    |   @    |    @    |    *    

Interpretation: high residual hotspots at short sessions at mid-to-high concurrency; also mid-length sessions at very high concurrency show catastrophic residuals (KV cache leakage + tiling thrash).

Residual decomposition (sketch):
- Predicted components: model decode time + network + base batch slot amortization.
- Observed extra: prefix miss (KV rebuild), preempt-induced serialization, small-batch decode penalties.

Small table: per-cause estimated contribution (ms) for SHORT-BURST cohort
- KV rebuild (cold prefixes): 180±40 ms
- Small-batch overhead (per-request): 30±10 ms
- Preemption wait: 90±35 ms
- Network variance: 20±12 ms
- Misc (scheduling jitter): 15±8 ms

Experiment sketch: routing shim that prefers edge-affinity for users with high short-burst rate, plus session-length-aware tiling (reserve micro-tiling slots for <120-token sessions). Sim assumptions: affinity reduces KV rebuilds by 70% for targeted cohort; tiling reduces small-batch overhead by 60%.

Estimated impact (simulation):
- SHORT-BURST p99: 890ms -> 740ms (17% drop)
- SHORT-BURST $/1k_tokens: 0.95 -> 0.88 (7% drop when amortized across session)
- Overall cluster p99: -3.2% (small, because SHORT-BURST is small fraction)

Sampling plan for next sprint:
1) Implement lightweight label emitter: mark sessions with >3 reqs in 30s and total tokens <120 (add sampling flag in request meta). (owner: Jasper)
2) Deploy routing shim in staging (edge affinity ON for labeled sessions). Measure KV hit-rate, rebuild counts. (owner: Priya)
3) Prototype tiling reservation (slot scheduler tweak) for small sessions. (owner: Rina)
4) Add evaluation dashboard: burst residual cohort, p99 change, cost delta. Hook to existing percentile alarms. (owner: Maya)

Open questions / caveats:
- Simulation assumed independent effect sizes; interactions (tiling + affinity) might yield non-linear gains or contention side-effects. Need AB tests.
- Cost proxy ($/1k tokens) used internal amortization constants from Feb 2028; re-run with updated GPU pricing if we plan to present externally.
- This approach focuses on residuals relative to our steady-state model; some residuals are expected from atypical model tokens (e.g., multimodal attachments) — must filter out outliers in dataset.

Notes to self:
- Add per-tenant breakdown next pass; hypothesize some tenants are overrepresented in SHORT-BURST.
- Consider coupling with predictive-prefetch: if we can predict short bursts within 1st request, we can prewarm KV cheaply.
- Put a short-form slide for Eng Review meeting: 3 bullets, 1 heatband, 1 action item.

Files / experiments to reference in PR:
- bench/run-heatband-replay-20280517.log (staging runner)
- scripts/affinity-sim.py (toy sim)
